small_guidance:
- The kernel uses `tl.atomic_max` per (M,N) tile which serializes writes across N-tiles for the same row. Switch to a two-stage strategy: emit per-tile partial maxes to a `(num_m_tiles, num_n_tiles)` scratch buffer, then a tiny second kernel reduces along the N-tile axis. This removes atomic contention and lets larger BLOCK_N tiles run freely.
- Add autotune configs with BLOCK_N=1024 (e.g. BLOCK_M=32/BLOCK_N=1024/BLOCK_K=64, num_warps=8, num_stages=3) — with N=8192 a wider N tile reduces the number of K-loops launched and grows POOLED_BLOCK_N=64 for a stronger in-tile max.
- Drop the masked loads on the inner K loop (M=1024, K=8192, N=8192 are all multiples of common block sizes); use unmasked `tl.load` and only mask the boundary tile to cut predicate overhead in the hot loop.
large_guidance:
- Restructure as a persistent split-K-free GEMM where each program owns one full row tile (BLOCK_M rows × full N) and streams N in chunks, maintaining a running scalar max per row in registers. This eliminates atomics entirely and fuses pool+GELU+scale+max into a single pass with no scratch tensor. With M=1024 and BLOCK_M=16-32, the grid is small enough for persistent scheduling on a 4090.
- Alternatively, use a two-kernel design: (1) tiled GEMM writing pooled+GELU+scale output of shape (M, N/POOL_K)=(1024, 512) via a standard non-atomic store, (2) a fast row-max kernel. This decouples the matmul tuning from the reduction and lets the matmul use wide BLOCK_N without atomic serialization, at the cost of one extra 2MB write/read.
- Consider fp16/bf16 accumulation inputs (cast x and weight_T to bf16 once at init) to leverage tensor cores on the 4090; current fp32 `tl.dot` runs at a fraction of peak. Keep accumulator fp32. This typically yields 2-3× on K=N=8192 GEMMs.
